contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Transfer the aggregate or potential proof only when each entry has a bounded number of constant-work transitions; count any attached scan, copy, or nonconstant work separately.

authoringProvenance.author: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Pro — candidate authoring assistant; human review required

items.prompt: A left-to-right next-greater scan pushes each of n indices once and never reinserts a popped index. One late value may pop a frontier of Θ(n) indices. Why does this not make the whole scan quadratic?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: Those entries cannot be popped again if each is pushed once and never reinserted.
A nested while loop always implies O(n²).
A loop nested inside the scan makes the total cost quadratic regardless of how many times each entry can actually be removed.
The maximum stack size multiplied by the input length is always the exact running time, independent of the executed operations.

feedback.reason: The expensive iteration consumes distinct entries permanently; across the run there are at most n pushes and n pops.

blocks.text: Label each input index. It is pushed once and, after a qualifying value pops it, never reappears. Therefore the entire execution contains at most `n` pushes and `n` pops, plus `n` outer visits and constant failed/terminal comparisons. A single iteration may cost Θ(n), but those same pops cannot recur in later iterations, so the aggregate is Θ(n) when each transition is constant time. Multiplying peak stack size by `n` counts operations that never execute.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Nested syntax permits quadratic work but does not prove it; the inner-loop iterations are globally limited by unique removals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: This repeats the same syntactic heuristic and ignores that each index can fund only one successful pop.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Peak occupancy and transition count are different quantities; a size-n frontier can be destroyed only once under the stated lifecycle.

items.prompt: Order the aggregate-accounting steps for a complete monotonic-stack trace.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: Charge at most one later pop to that same occurrence.
Add the O(1) outer-scan work performed for each input occurrence.
Bound total work by O(n) scan steps plus at most n pushes and n pops.
Give every input occurrence a stable identity.
Count one push when each occurrence first becomes a candidate.

feedback.reason: Stable identities let the proof charge one push and at most one pop to each occurrence, then add the n outer visits.

items: Label each of the `n` input occurrences with a stable identity.
Charge one push to each identity when it first becomes a candidate.
Charge at most one later pop to that same identity.
Add one constant outer-scan visit per occurrence.
Sum `n pushes + at most n pops + O(n) visits = O(n)`.

blocks.text: Assigning a possible `n` pops independently to every iteration invents repeated removals forbidden by the lifecycle.

items.prompt: A next-greater scan processes n items. Each item is pushed once, popped at most once, and every comparison, push, pop, and answer write is O(1). What is the total time complexity?
constraints: Count the operations stated in the prompt; do not infer a complexity from the stack label alone.
Treat arithmetic, comparison, push, pop, and one answer write as O(1) unless the prompt explicitly attaches larger work.

feedback.reason: At most n pushes, n pops, and constant scan work per item sum to O(n).

blocks.text: There are exactly `n` outer visits and at most `n` pushes. Because an item disappears permanently after its pop, there are at most `n` pops and answer writes. With constant work per stated operation, `c1*n + c2*n + c3*n = O(n)`. The answer is not `O(1)` because all inputs are read, and not `O(n²)` because a Θ(n)-pop iteration consumes the finite pop budget rather than repeating it.

items.prompt: A scan assigns each input occurrence a stable identity, pushes it at most once, and never reinserts it after pop. Which analysis correctly determines total stack-transition work?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: The maximum stack size multiplied by the input length is always the exact running time, independent of the executed operations.
Count total pushes and irreversible pops over the entire run.
Analyze each loop iteration in isolation.
A loop nested inside the scan makes the total cost quadratic regardless of how many times each entry can actually be removed.

feedback.reason: The correct aggregate counts each occurrence’s bounded lifecycle over the whole execution, not an isolated worst case per iteration.

blocks.text: With `n` identities, at most `n` pushes and `n` irreversible pops can execute. An iteration-by-iteration worst-case multiplication treats the same identity as if it could be popped repeatedly, contradicting the prompt. Multiplying maximum occupancy by input length has the same flaw. This proves only transition count; any search, copy, or other work inside a transition must still be added separately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Local worst cases overlap in the same finite set of candidates and cannot be summed as independent events.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The nested loop is linear here because its successful iterations are unique pops, not because nesting is irrelevant in general.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Maximum live size does not say how often entries transition; the exact execution contains at most `2n` such transitions.

items.prompt: Select all valid charging assignments for the constant work in a monotonic-stack pop loop.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Ignore work performed during pops because only pushes count toward amortized analysis.
Charge each pop to the unique candidate entry that is removed.
Use the fact that one candidate can be removed at most once after being pushed once.
Include the constant comparison and answer-write work associated with that removal in the same charge.
Charge n units to every outer-loop iteration because the inner loop could be long in isolation.

feedback.reason: Charge each removal and its constant comparison/write work to the unique candidate that can be removed only once.

blocks.text: Give each pushed candidate one account. Its later pop, comparison, and one answer write are charged to that account. Because the candidate cannot be popped again, each account pays constant work once, totaling O(n). Charging `n` to every outer iteration duplicates the same potential pops, while ignoring pop work omits real operations. The proof stops applying if the pop body copies or scans nonconstant state.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: It charges hypothetical pops independently even though each candidate can fund only one actual removal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Pops, comparisons, and answer writes execute and must be counted; amortization redistributes cost rather than erasing it.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: It assigns every successful inner-loop iteration to one identifiable owner.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: It bounds each owner's total charge by one removal after one insertion.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: It includes all constant operations caused by that removal instead of counting only the API call.

items.prompt: Order a potential-method proof using Φ = current stack size.
constraints: Order the steps by semantic dependency, not by the order in which they are listed.
The canonical scoring contract awards preserved adjacent relations.

elements.text: A push performs O(1) actual work and increases Φ by 1, storing one unit of potential.
A pop performs O(1) actual work and decreases Φ by 1, releasing stored potential to pay for the pop.
Combine actual work and potential change to bound each processed input by O(1) amortized stack-transition cost.
Sum over n inputs and use nonnegative initial/final potential to obtain O(n) total transition work.
Define the nonnegative potential Φ as the current number of retained entries.

feedback.reason: With Φ equal to stack size, a push stores one unit and each pop releases one; `actual + ΔΦ` cancels any number of pops in one input step.

items: Define nonnegative potential `Φ = stack size`, initially zero.
A push costs one constant unit and raises `Φ` by one.
Each pop costs one constant unit and lowers `Φ` by one.
For `p` pops plus one push, amortized work is `(p + 1) + ΔΦ = (p + 1) + (1 - p) = 2`.
Sum over n inputs; telescoping nonnegative potential yields O(n) total transition work.

blocks.text: A negative potential or a nonconstant pop body would invalidate this payment argument.

items.prompt: Across a complete n-item monotonic-stack scan, total constant-time stack-transition work is O(n). What is the amortized stack-transition cost per processed input item?
constraints: Count the operations stated in the prompt; do not infer a complexity from the stack label alone.
Treat arithmetic, comparison, push, pop, and one answer write as O(1) unless the prompt explicitly attaches larger work.

feedback.reason: Total transition work O(n) divided across n processed inputs gives amortized O(1).

blocks.text: Amortized cost is the total cost of a sequence divided across its operations, not a bound on every individual operation. Here `O(n) / n = O(1)` amortized per input. One input may still perform Θ(n) actual pops, paid for by many earlier inputs that pushed those entries. `O(n)` amortized per input would imply an unsupported O(n²) total, while `O(log n)` has no source in the stated lifecycle.

items.prompt: A modified algorithm allows a popped candidate to be reinserted during later oscillations instead of being permanently removed. Can the usual push-once/pop-once linear proof be reused?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: The maximum stack size multiplied by the input length is always the exact running time, independent of the executed operations.
An entry that can re-enter may be charged and popped repeatedly.
The stack API alone preserves push-once/pop-once.
A loop nested inside the scan makes the total cost quadratic regardless of how many times each entry can actually be removed.

feedback.reason: No: reinsertion lets the same identity incur repeated pushes and pops, so the one-charge-per-entry bound is gone.

blocks.text: The ordinary linear proof depends on identity lifecycle, not on the stack API: each candidate is inserted once and permanently removed at most once. If a removed identity may re-enter after each oscillation, one candidate can pay Θ(n) transitions and many candidates may do so, allowing Θ(n²) work. A nested loop is not automatically quadratic, but here the bounded-transition premise has explicitly failed. A fresh proof must bound reinsertions or expose the larger cost.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: A stack does not enforce identity uniqueness; the algorithm's reinsertion rule determines the transition bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: Loop nesting alone still proves nothing, but repeated identity transitions now make superlinear work genuinely possible.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Peak size times n is not automatically exact; the correct objection is the loss of a bounded per-identity lifecycle.

items.prompt: Select all operations that can make a stack algorithm superlinear even when each entry is pushed and popped at most once.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: Compare the current key with the top in O(1) time before a possible pop.
Write one O(1) answer for the unique candidate being finalized.
Linearly search the entire retained stack for every new input item.
Copy a growing stack or list whenever an entry is popped.
Attach a nonconstant nested scan to each otherwise bounded transition.

feedback.reason: A linear number of stack transitions is insufficient when each visit, pop, or removal can carry growing extra work.

blocks.text: Searching a frontier of size Θ(n) for each of n inputs gives Θ(n²). Copying remaining sizes `n-1, n-2, ..., 0` across one pop cascade sums to Θ(n²). A nonconstant scan attached to each of Θ(n) transitions likewise multiplies the cost. In contrast, one O(1) top comparison and one O(1) answer write per unique removal remain covered by the linear charge.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: One constant comparison per visit or pop contributes only O(n) across a linear transition count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: One constant write per uniquely finalized candidate also totals O(n).

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: A full search per input independently contributes up to n work on n visits.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: Growing copies sum over changing stack sizes even though each candidate is popped once.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: A bounded transition count does not bound a nonconstant body attached to every transition.

items.prompt: An implementation still pushes and pops each candidate at most once, but on every pop it copies the entire remaining stack. A final input may pop Θ(n) entries from a stack of decreasing sizes. What is the worst-case total time?
constraints: Count the operations stated in the prompt; do not infer a complexity from the stack label alone.
Treat arithmetic, comparison, push, pop, and one answer write as O(1) unless the prompt explicitly attaches larger work.

feedback.reason: Amortization bounds the number of pops, not arbitrary work attached to each pop.

blocks.text: The final cascade performs Θ(n) pops, but the copies cost `(n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 + 0 = n(n-1)/2 = Θ(n²)`. Earlier scan and push work is only O(n), so the total is Θ(n²), represented by accepted `O(n²)`. `O(n)` counts pop events but ignores their growing bodies; `O(n³)` would require another independent factor of n.

items.prompt: Delimiter validation processes each token once with at most one matching pop per closer. Next-greater processing may pop many candidates in one iteration but pushes and pops each index at most once. What follows?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: A loop nested inside the scan makes the total cost quadratic regardless of how many times each entry can actually be removed.
The maximum stack size multiplied by the input length is always the exact running time, independent of the executed operations.
Both can be O(n) for different transition semantics; Big-O does not identify the variant.
Only monotonic stacks receive amortized linear bounds.

feedback.reason: Both are O(n), but delimiter pops follow structural matches while next-greater linearity uses an aggregate candidate-lifecycle proof.

blocks.text: Delimiter validation has n token visits and each opener is pushed and matched at most once. Next-greater has n visits, at most n pushes, and at most n irreversible pops even though a single visit can be expensive. Both totals are O(n), but their retained meanings and pop triggers differ. Therefore complexity class cannot classify the stack variant, and a nested-loop sighting cannot override the executed-operation count.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: Ordinary delimiter entries also have a bounded push/pop lifecycle, so their total is linear.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The monotonic inner loop is globally bounded by unique pops and does not imply quadratic time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Peak size multiplied by n invents repeated transitions in both algorithms.

items.prompt: An undo-history algorithm pushes n actions. After each push it scans the entire current stack to answer a query. What is the total time over all n actions?
constraints: Count the operations stated in the prompt; do not infer a complexity from the stack label alone.
Treat arithmetic, comparison, push, pop, and one answer write as O(1) unless the prompt explicitly attaches larger work.

feedback.reason: Ordinary/monotonic labels do not fix complexity; actual operations do.

blocks.text: After push i, the stack contains i actions and the query scans i entries. Total scan work is `1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 = Θ(n²)`; the n constant pushes do not change the dominant term. The answer is not O(n) merely because the container is an ordinary stack, and no logarithmic factor appears in the stated full scans.

items.prompt: Select all input/rule combinations that can force Θ(n) retained entries.
constraints: Select all and only the statements that remain valid under the exact output and tie policy.
Each selected statement must be justified by retained-state semantics or a correctness/cost argument.

options.text: An ordinary delimiter stack after n unmatched opening tokens.
Next-greater search on a strictly increasing input, where each new value resolves recent smaller candidates.
A stack that is explicitly cleared after every processed item by the contract.
Next-greater search with a decreasing candidate stack on a strictly decreasing input.
Next-smaller search with an increasing candidate stack on a strictly increasing input.

feedback.reason: When no input satisfies the pop predicate—or no closer arrives—all n entries can remain live simultaneously.

blocks.text: For next greater, strictly decreasing input never makes `current > top`, so all n candidates accumulate. For next smaller, strictly increasing input never makes `current < top`, with the same result. n unmatched opening delimiters also remain pending. Strictly increasing next-greater input repeatedly resolves the previous top and keeps the frontier small, while an explicit clear-after-each-item contract caps occupancy independently of n.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_1: Each larger current value resolves recent smaller candidates, so this direction does not force n simultaneous entries.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.false_claim_2: Clearing after every item caps the stack at a constant number of entries.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_1: No decreasing-input value resolves a larger previous top under next-greater semantics.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_2: No increasing-input value resolves a smaller previous top under next-smaller semantics.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.required_fact_3: Without closing tokens, every opener remains structurally unmatched.

items.prompt: Compare two worst cases: n unmatched opening tokens in an ordinary stack, and n candidates that receive no next-greater resolution in a monotonic stack. What is the worst-case auxiliary space in either case?
constraints: Count the operations stated in the prompt; do not infer a complexity from the stack label alone.
Treat arithmetic, comparison, push, pop, and one answer write as O(1) unless the prompt explicitly attaches larger work.

feedback.reason: Both may retain n unmatched/pending/candidate entries, so worst-case extra space is O(n).

blocks.text: n unmatched openers require n live delimiter entries. Likewise, an input that never resolves a next-greater candidate leaves n `(value,index)` entries live. Each entry is constant size, so peak auxiliary storage is `n * O(1) = O(n)`. Amortized O(1) transition time per input does not imply O(1) space; time counts lifecycle events, while space measures simultaneous retention.

items.prompt: A circular next-greater algorithm performs exactly `2n` visits, pushes each original index at most once, pops it at most once, and does O(1) work per visit or transition. What total-time argument is valid?
constraints: Use the exact output, strictness, scan direction, and tie semantics stated in the prompt.
Do not classify the algorithm from a variable name or one intermediate snapshot.

options.text: A loop nested inside the scan makes the total cost quadratic regardless of how many times each entry can actually be removed.
The maximum stack size multiplied by the input length is always the exact running time, independent of the executed operations.
A constant number of n-length passes remains O(n) when entries are not pushed unboundedly.
Any second pass makes the algorithm quadratic.

feedback.reason: Two bounded passes contribute `2n` visits, and the one-push/one-pop lifecycle contributes O(n) more transitions, so total time is O(n).

blocks.text: The visits cost `2n = O(n)`. Across both passes, stable original identities permit at most n pushes and n pops, each constant time. Thus the sum remains O(n). A second pass adds rather than multiplies n when its count is fixed; quadratic behavior would require n passes, repeated reinsertion, or nonconstant work inside visits.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.target_false_heuristic: `n + n = 2n`, not `n * n`; a fixed second pass preserves linear asymptotics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.surface_feature_classifier: The inner pop loop is bounded across both passes by at most n unique removals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unjustified_alternative_rule: Peak size times visits is not the executed work; each identity has a bounded transition count.

items.prompt: An algorithm performs k = 4 independent directional boundary passes. Each pass scans n items and uses amortized O(1) stack-transition work per item. What is the simplified total time complexity?
constraints: Count the operations stated in the prompt; do not infer a complexity from the stack label alone.
Treat arithmetic, comparison, push, pop, and one answer write as O(1) unless the prompt explicitly attaches larger work.

feedback.reason: A fixed product constant does not change asymptotic linearity; growing k must remain explicit.

blocks.text: Each pass costs `n * O(1) amortized = O(n)`. Four independent passes cost `4 * O(n) = O(4n)`, which simplifies to O(n) because 4 is fixed. O(1) ignores reading the inputs, O(n log n) introduces an absent logarithmic operation, and O(n²) would require the number of passes or per-item work to grow with n. If `k` were input-dependent, the unsimplified bound would be O(kn).
